Economic activity expanded modestly, but the policy stance turned more restrictive as the FOMC lifted the federal funds target to 5–5.25% and continued quantitative tightening. Consistent with the credit channel literature (e.g., Bernanke’s emphasis on agency costs and broad credit), tighter bank lending conditions tend to amplify the real effects of higher rates, implying a larger drag on business investment and hiring than the policy rate alone would suggest. The Committee’s focus on cumulative tightening and lags accords with New Keynesian policy-rule frameworks (Taylor/Woodford), indicating that the peak growth slowdown likely lies ahead. At the same time, a clear commitment to the 2% objective and systematic implementation (including ON RRP at 5.05% and ongoing Treasury/MBS runoff) support the anchoring of inflation expectations in the spirit of inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson, Woodford), which should temper inflation persistence even with sticky-information frictions (Mankiw–Reis). Balance sheet runoff and higher money-market rates also work through the term structure to raise term premia, reinforcing restraint on demand. With the banking system described as sound, systemic risk appears contained, but the balance of risks skews toward softer growth and gradually cooling inflation. Overall tone: slightly negative for the growth outlook, cautiously constructive for disinflation.
